name: ArtifactsBench
description: ArtifactsBench is a benchmark and automated, multimodal evaluation paradigm for visual code generation. It comprises 1,825 diverse executable tasks across nine domains (Game Development, SVG Generation, Web Applications, Simulations, Data Science, Management Systems, Multimedia Editing, Quick Tools, and Others), stratified into Easy/Medium/Hard tiers. The framework renders each artifact and captures its dynamic behavior via temporal (three-step) screenshots, assessed by a Multimodal LLM (MLLM)-as-Judge guided by fine-grained, per-task checklists. It evaluates over 30 leading LLMs and achieves 94.4% ranking consistency with WebDev Arena and up to 90.95% pairwise agreement with human experts.
creator: Tencent Hunyuan Team
citeAs: Tencent Hunyuan Team. ArtifactsBench: Bridging the Visual-Interactive Gap in LLM Code Generation Evaluation. arXiv:2507.04952v2 [cs.CL], 2025.
rai:dataCollection: Tasks were aggregated from expert showcases, open SVG/web-snippet datasets, web case studies, and LLM visual-to-query from screenshots. Automated filters dropped incomplete, non-visual, license-violating, duplicate, trivial, or non-interactive items, prioritizing dynamics (state changes, animations, responsiveness). Experts rewrote prompts for clarity, completeness, and executability; LLM rewriting added diverse styles; humans verified. Each query was paired with a 10-dimension checklist covering visual, interactional, and code qualities, LLM-drafted and then human-refined. Solvability validation was performed by collecting candidate solutions from multiple model families and pruning underspecified items.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping, Software Collection, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Candidates were aggregated from expert showcases, open SVG/web-snippet datasets, web case studies, and LLM visual-to-query generation from screenshots.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Two-stage de-duplication and contamination control: (i) MinHash plus semantic similarity over prompts, checklists, and normalized DOM/CSS/JS; (ii) screenshot perceptual hashing to catch visually near-identical artifacts. Flagged items were re-authored or discarded. Difficulty was assigned post hoc by aggregated performance of 30+ models to enforce a 30%/40%/30% Easy/Medium/Hard split. Sub-categories were tagged by a lightweight classifier with human spot-checks.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Automated filters dropped incomplete, non-visual, license-violating, duplicate, trivial, or non-interactive items. Prompts were rewritten by experts for clarity, completeness, and executability, with LLM rewriting adding diverse styles and human verification. Tasks solved only by brittle hacks were revised or removed. Execution was standardized with headless Chromium (Playwright) at 1024x768 resolution and deterministic seeds, capturing three staged screenshots (before/during/after scripted interaction).
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Each query was paired with a 10-dimension checklist covering visual, interactional, and code qualities. Checklists were LLM-drafted (using Hunyuan-Turbos) and then human-refined for specificity and screenability. A 10% manually curated seed anchored calibration and achieved Cohen's kappa >= 0.8 among annotators; the seed was reused as few-shot references. The 10 items were grouped into five vision-oriented and five code-oriented dimensions. For human validation, 280 queries with outputs from 6 models were independently scored by multiple front-end engineers in a double-blind protocol; the final human ground-truth score represents the median of individual annotators' ratings.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Checklist calibration achieved Cohen's kappa >= 0.8 among annotators on a 10% manually curated seed set. Automated referee agreement with human experts was measured by pairwise consistency rate (Pair ACC), achieving up to 90.95% with Gemini-2.5-Pro using multiple screenshots. Cross-judge robustness was validated by comparing Gemini-2.5-Pro and Qwen2.5-VL-72B, which induced highly consistent partial-order constraints over model rankings. Version stability was confirmed by comparing deprecated Gemini-2.5-Pro-Preview-0506 with stable Gemini-2.5-Pro, yielding identical ordering constraints.
rai:annotationsPerItem: 10 checklist dimensions per query; 280 queries were additionally scored by multiple human front-end engineers
rai:annotatorDemographics: Multiple engineers with extensive front-end development experience
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Gemini-2.5-Pro (MLLM-as-Judge referee), Qwen2.5-VL-72B (MLLM-as-Judge referee), Hunyuan-Turbos (checklist generation), Gemini-2.5-Pro (query classification), Playwright (headless Chromium for artifact execution and screenshot capture)
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: ArtifactsBench is open-sourced including the benchmark, evaluation harness, and baseline results at https://artifactsbenchmark.github.io. Dataset specs, checklist templates, evaluation scripts, and referee settings are released. Future work targets richer dynamics beyond discrete screenshots, agentic multi-turn self-debugging, and broader artifact domains.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The quality filtering prompt explicitly checks for privacy: queries must avoid requesting or involving any sensitive personal information, such as phone numbers, addresses, or other identifiable details.
rai:dataSocialImpact: ArtifactsBench provides the community with a scalable and accurate tool to accelerate the development of user-centric generative models. By enabling automated, holistic evaluation of interactive visual artifacts, it aims to advance LLM capabilities in producing high-fidelity, functional interactive experiences central to modern user applications.
rai:dataBiases: The benchmark currently focuses on evaluating the quality of the final artifact generated in a single turn, which does not assess agentic or iterative development capabilities. The discrete screenshot sampling approach may not fully capture the fluidity, correctness, and robustness of highly complex, long-horizon, or state-dependent interactions. Minor discrepancies between referee models are observed in fine-grained scoring of certain complex interactive tasks, reflecting potential cognitive biases in how different MLLMs interpret long-horizon interaction logic and dynamic visual feedback.
rai:dataLimitations: The current methodology evaluates dynamic behavior by capturing screenshots at fixed intervals, which may not fully capture the fluidity, correctness, and robustness of highly complex, long-horizon, or state-dependent interactions (e.g., multi-step user workflows, nuanced physics in games). The benchmark focuses on single-turn artifact generation and does not assess agentic capabilities such as iterative refinement, self-debugging, or multi-step development. MLLM referees can suffer from hallucination, prompt sensitivity, limited awareness of engineering/code quality, and version drift.
rai:dataUseCases: Testing and evaluation of LLMs on interactive visual code generation tasks. The benchmark supports fine-grained capability analysis across nine domains and three difficulty tiers (Easy/Medium/Hard), diagnostic analysis of model strengths and failure modes, and ranking of 30+ LLMs. It is intended as a scalable evaluation tool for advancing user-centric generative models in web development, SVG generation, game development, simulations, data science, and related domains.
